canterbury.intro: Canterbury's strangest trees are its baobab planes, a scattered set of seven whose trunks swell outward like the African tree's. Four of them are here. The biggest, beside Tower House in Westgate Gardens, is about 200 years old and 7.6 metres round; the others stand at the castle ruins, in the cathedral precincts and beside a bus stop on Old Dover Road. Nobody agrees what they are, Oriental Planes by the plaques or a virus-swollen London Plane clone by the Natural History Museum, nor quite who planted them.
canterbury.meta_description: Canterbury's four baobab planes, swollen-trunked trees in Westgate Gardens, at the castle, the cathedral and Old Dover Road, and what they really are.
canterbury.question_meta: The oldest tree we map in Canterbury is the Westgate Gardens baobab plane, about 200 years old, its trunk 7.6 metres round beside Tower House.
canterbury.question_answer: The oldest tree we map in Canterbury is the baobab plane beside Tower House in Westgate Gardens, about 200 years old by the accounts of Visit Canterbury and Parks and Gardens. Its swollen trunk is about 7.6 metres round. It stands in a free public park by the River Stour, five minutes on foot from Canterbury West station.
canterbury.question_context: Canterbury has seven plane trees with trunks so swollen that locals named them after the baobab, and the one in Westgate Gardens is the largest. The gardens' tree trail calls it the biggest and probably the oldest of its kind in the country, a local claim that no national register confirms. What kind it is remains disputed. Plaques in the gardens and at the cathedral call these trees Oriental Planes, as did the city's archaeological society at first. In 2014 the Natural History Museum's identification service told the society that the set is a clone of the London Plane carrying a viral infection. Their origin is just as loose. A plaque credits the nurseryman William Masters, who lived from 1796 to 1874, with supplying the cathedral's tree in the 1820s, but one society member has said that wording came from the society's own website rather than from an archive. A further local theory holds that the Westgate tree is the parent of the others, and another that the seven form a cross on the map. Neither has been proved. KentOnline puts the planes at more than 150 years old, so every age here stays broad.

faq.a: Seven plane trees scattered across Canterbury whose trunks swell outward like an African baobab's. Four are on this map: in Westgate Gardens, at the castle ruins, in the cathedral precincts and on Old Dover Road.

faq.q: Are they Oriental Planes or London Planes?
faq.a: Sources differ. Plaques and early accounts call them Oriental Planes; in 2014 the Natural History Museum's identification service concluded they are a clone of the London Plane with a viral infection.

faq.q: Can you see them for free?
faq.a: Three of the four, yes. Westgate Gardens, the castle grounds and the pavement on Old Dover Road cost nothing. The cathedral precincts are ticketed.

Local tradition credits the nurseryman William Masters, who lived from 1796 to 1874, and the Cathedral Archive recognises him for the precincts tree. No archive record of the plantings has been published.

stratford-upon-avon.intro: Stratford-upon-Avon's two old mulberries both grow in gardens of the Shakespeare family. The one at New Place, where the poet's last home stood, is believed to have grown from a cutting of the mulberry he is said to have planted, which was felled in 1756; the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust puts it at around 270 years. The other, in the garden of Hall's Croft, where his daughter Susanna lived, grows almost sideways through a flower bed. Both stand in ticketed Trust gardens a short walk apart in the Old Town.
stratford-upon-avon.meta_description: Two old mulberries in Stratford-upon-Avon, one at New Place believed grown from a cutting of Shakespeare's own tree, one growing sideways at Hall's Croft.
stratford-upon-avon.question_meta: The New Place mulberry, around 270 years old by the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust's estimate, is the oldest tree we map in Stratford-upon-Avon.
stratford-upon-avon.question_answer: The oldest tree we map in Stratford-upon-Avon is the black mulberry in the Great Garden at New Place, around 270 years old by the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust's estimate. The Trust believes it grew from a cutting of the mulberry Shakespeare is said to have planted, which was felled in 1756. It stands in a ticketed garden on Chapel Street in the Old Town.
stratford-upon-avon.question_context: Shakespeare's mulberry is one of the most retold tree stories in England, and almost every part of it is tradition. The poet is said to have planted a mulberry at New Place, his last home in Stratford. In 1756 the Reverend Francis Gastrell cut it down. The wood did not go to waste: a chair dated 1862 is said to have been made from it. What grows in the Great Garden today is a black mulberry the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust believes was raised from a cutting of the felled tree, and its estimate of around 270 years fits a cutting taken soon after 1756. The Trust's blog described it in 2013 as a venerable and massive tree still bearing fruit, and the Trust now harvests the fruit for a New Place Mulberry Gin Liqueur. A younger mulberry in the same garden was planted by Dame Peggy Ashcroft in 1969 and split in 2013. Across the Old Town, the garden of Hall's Croft holds a third mulberry whose trunk runs almost horizontally through a flower bed. Nobody has published its age, and the most recent account of it dates from 2013.

faq.q: Is the New Place mulberry Shakespeare's own tree?
faq.a: Not the tree itself, which was felled in 1756. The Shakespeare Birthplace Trust believes the mulberry in the Great Garden grew from a cutting of it, and puts its age at around 270 years. The link is tradition rather than proof.
Yes, both stand in Shakespeare Birthplace Trust gardens with paid entry, New Place on Chapel Street and Hall's Croft near Holy Trinity Church. Check the Trust's site for hours and prices.

faq.q: When does the New Place mulberry fruit?
faq.a: In July and August. The Trust harvests the fruit for its New Place Mulberry Gin Liqueur.

faq.q: What is unusual about the Hall's Croft mulberry?
faq.a: Its trunk grows almost horizontally through a flower bed. The Shakespeare Birthplace Trust's blog noted in 2013 that old mulberries tend to lean and split with age.

mottisfont.intro: Mottisfont, a National Trust estate in the Test valley near Romsey, has one tree on this map, and it is a big one. The Great Plane of Mottisfont stands close to a house that began as an Augustinian priory in the early 13th century, and Wikipedia calls it the largest London plane in Britain. OpenStreetMap records it at about 30 metres tall. Its age has not been confirmed. Entry is paid, free to Trust members, and the nearest station is Dunbridge, about 1.5 kilometres away.
mottisfont.meta_description: The Great Plane of Mottisfont, called the largest London plane in Britain, beside a National Trust house near Romsey that began as a 13th-century priory.
mottisfont.question_meta: Wikipedia names the Great Plane of Mottisfont, near Romsey in Hampshire, as the largest London plane in Britain. It stands about 30 metres tall.
mottisfont.question_answer: The largest London plane in Britain, according to Wikipedia, is the Great Plane of Mottisfont, on the National Trust's Mottisfont estate near Romsey in Hampshire. OpenStreetMap records it at about 30 metres tall. It stands close to the house, inside the paid estate, about 1.5 kilometres from Dunbridge station.
mottisfont.question_context: Most people meet London planes as street trees, a row of trunks along a pavement. The Great Plane of Mottisfont is what one becomes with a whole estate to itself. It grows beside a house in the Test valley that was founded as an Augustinian priory in the early 13th century and turned into a country house after Henry VIII dissolved the monasteries, now looked after by the National Trust. Wikipedia names it the largest London plane in Britain, and OpenStreetMap maps it by name as a landmark about 30 metres tall. Tree recorders have reported a greater height, a much larger girth and a planting in the 18th century, and those figures may well hold, but they have not yet been confirmed. Until they are, the tree's age is an open question. Getting there takes some planning. The nearest station, Dunbridge, is about 1.5 kilometres away, and the journey from Winchester involves a change of train.

faq.q: Where is the largest London plane in Britain?
faq.a: According to Wikipedia, at Mottisfont, the National Trust estate near Romsey in Hampshire. The Great Plane of Mottisfont stands close to the house.

faq.q: How old is the Great Plane of Mottisfont?
faq.a: Its age has not been confirmed. Reports of an 18th-century planting circulate but are unverified, so the question is open.
No, Mottisfont charges admission. National Trust members get in free.

faq.q: Can you reach Mottisfont by train?
faq.a: Yes. The nearest station is Dunbridge, about 1.5 kilometres from the house. From Winchester the journey needs a change of train.

oxford.intro: Oxford's most remarkable trees mostly belong to its colleges and gardens rather than open woodland. They include a churchyard yew possibly older than the Norman church beside it, the yew Britain's first botanic garden curator planted in 1645, and a plane grown, so the story goes, from a seed a Hebrew professor carried back from the Ottoman Empire in 1636. Add two mulberries, a white one that may be the oldest of its kind in Britain and Balliol's hollow black mulberry, said to date from 1609 and still fruiting, plus the country's tallest Caucasian elm, all inside a short walk.
oxford.meta_description: Oxford's remarkable trees: the Iffley churchyard yew, Christ Church's Jabberwocky plane, the 1645 Bobart yew and Balliol's mulberry of about 1609.

cambridge.intro: Cambridge's remarkable trees split between college gardens and the University Botanic Garden. The colleges hold a mulberry that grew back from its own roots after a 1795 storm, an apple grafted in 1954 from the tree behind Newton's theory of gravity, and a plane raised from seed carried home from Thermopylae. The Botanic Garden adds a redwood from the first seed shipped out of California, a one-off hybrid oak, black pines Darwin's teacher planted to look mismatched, a wingnut that became a thicket after an 1886 storm, and a 1949 dawn redwood.
cambridge.meta_description: Cambridge's remarkable trees: the Milton Mulberry, Trinity's Newton apple graft, Henslow's black pines and the Botanic Garden's 1949 dawn redwood.
